central_question: By 2040, will annual global grid-scale energy-storage additions reach at least 300 GW, and will non-lithium long-duration storage capture at least 20% of annual added GWh; if not, which lower-growth or lithium-dominant regime will prevail?

situation_brief.current_situation: Global battery-storage additions reached 112 GW and 307 GWh in 2025, an average duration of 2.74 hours, and the cited BloombergNEF outlook projects 158 GW of additions in 2026. LFP remains the bankable default for four-hour projects, supported by Chinese manufacturers holding about 85% of cell-manufacturing capacity and Chinese integrators about 76% of the 2025 BESS market. China reported 136 GW and 351 GWh of commissioned new-type storage at end-2025, although a CNESA series reported 144.7 GW, while non-lithium technologies still lack multiple large commercial reference projects with long operating histories. The central constraint has shifted from cell availability toward interconnection, duration-sensitive capacity accreditation, contracted revenue, safety compliance, and conversion of announced projects into operating assets.
situation_brief.context: Lithium-ion pack prices fell by roughly 90% from about US$1,400/kWh in 2010 to below US$140/kWh in 2023, allowing LFP to accumulate manufacturing scale, warranties, EPC experience, financing templates, and operating references. As variable renewable penetration increased, storage deployment expanded faster than system operators redesigned interconnection and capacity rules, producing long queues, short average durations, and revenue cannibalization in early merchant markets. China subsequently moved from build mandates toward dispatch telemetry, utilization, and capacity compensation, while the United States, Europe, India, Australia, and the Gulf developed different combinations of queue reform, capacity markets, tolling contracts, local-content rules, and long-duration procurement.
situation_brief.dynamics: LFP cost and integration scale continue to accelerate four-hour deployment, but ancillary-service saturation and declining merchant revenue weaken the economics of adding more identical assets. Regulators and system operators are beginning to reward duration, which could move investment toward flow batteries, compressed-air, liquid-air, thermal storage, and iron-air, but these routes remain constrained by thin operating records and limited non-recourse financing. Trade and local-content rules are fragmenting the global cost curve, while Chinese overcapacity simultaneously lowers equipment prices and intensifies dependence on Chinese materials and integration. The dossier assigns 30% to Lithium Dominance, 25% to LDES Diversified, 20% to China-Centric Vertical, and 25% to Stagnation, but a later chart presents a conflicting 47%/29%/18%/6% weighting that must not be silently averaged.
fault_lines: Whether capacity markets and resource-adequacy rules should compensate duration and demonstrated availability rather than nameplate megawatts.
Whether LFP's system-integration and financing moat outweighs the architecture advantage of flow, compressed-air, thermal, liquid-air, and iron-air storage beyond eight hours.
Whether tariffs, FEOC restrictions, EU battery rules, and local-content mandates will diversify supply chains or mainly raise project costs and delay deployment.
How aggressively announced, tendered, or queued capacity should be discounted when historical completion rates and commissioning evidence are weak.
Whether safety, insurance, recycling, and siting requirements should be treated as necessary system costs or as barriers that disproportionately slow lithium-ion projects.
Whether public targets such as the IEA Net Zero trajectory and DOE LDES cost goals represent achievable deployment paths or policy aspirations unsupported by bankable cash flows.
catalysts: China reaching or missing the official 180 GW new-type-storage target by 2027, together with changes in average duration and equivalent utilization hours.
FERC Order 2023 cluster-study results in 2027–2028 showing whether queue withdrawals fall and application-to-operation lead times improve.
ERCOT post-RTC+B battery revenue recovering above US$120/kW-year or remaining below US$70/kW-year for two consecutive years.
PJM capacity auctions maintaining prices above US$200/MW-day while admitting materially more duration-accredited storage.
At least two non-lithium technologies commissioning at least 5 GWh of non-demonstration capacity in two consecutive years before 2030.
A technology-neutral 10-hour-plus capacity contract clearing at US$50–75/kW-year equivalent for at least 15 years in a major market.
A 100 MW-plus flow, compressed-air, liquid-air, thermal, or iron-air reference project publishing at least 12 months of third-party availability and efficiency data.
A major BESS fire, moratorium, or insurer rule materially increasing spacing, testing, or insurance costs.
US FEOC and tax-credit implementation either preserving project finance for storage or materially excluding Chinese-origin components.

actors.name: National Development and Reform Commission of China
actors.role: China's principal economic planner and a central designer of storage scale targets, market compensation, technology-development priorities, and dispatch policy.
actors.stance: Supports at least 180 GW of new-type storage by 2027, continued lithium-ion scale, commercialization of compressed-air, flow, and sodium-ion routes, and a shift from mandatory construction toward dispatchable and market-compensated operation.

salience.basis: It sets national targets and market rules in the country responsible for roughly half of current global storage additions.

actors.description: The National Development and Reform Commission is China's cabinet-level economic planning agency and co-author of the 2025–2027 new-type-storage scale-up program.
aliases: 国家发展和改革委员会
China National Development and Reform Commission
goals: Reach at least 180 GW of operational new-type storage by the end of 2027.
Convert storage from a build mandate into a dispatchable system resource with sustainable revenue.
Preserve Chinese industrial leadership while commercializing selected non-lithium technologies.
constraints: Provincial capacity-payment and market-access rules remain uneven.
Installed capacity does not automatically produce utilization or project-level returns.
Grid telemetry, safety, and dispatch compliance can delay market registration.
assets: Ability to coordinate investment targets and provincial implementation
vulnerabilities: A persistent gap between installed capacity and useful dispatch would undermine the policy shift.
Conflicting official capacity definitions weaken measurement and accountability.
Overbuilding short-duration LFP could deepen revenue cannibalization.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: The commission publicly promotes technology diversification, but the revealed scale strategy remains anchored overwhelmingly in lithium-ion while non-lithium routes are moved only gradually from demonstration toward commercialization.

beliefs: Storage must be observable, measurable, controllable, and compensated as a system resource.
Manufacturing capacity is no longer the principal constraint; utilization and market design are.
worldview.identity: National planner balancing rapid construction with system discipline and industrial policy.
worldview.frame: Storage is grid infrastructure and an industrial-development platform, not merely a collection of battery projects.

incentives.driver: Achievement of national reliability and industrial targets
incentives.gains_if: China exceeds 180 GW with rising duration, utilization, and domestic technology exports.
incentives.loses_if: Capacity grows while utilization, safety, or project economics deteriorate.

incentives.gains_if: Chinese firms commercialize sodium-ion, flow, and compressed-air without disrupting LFP scale.
incentives.loses_if: Foreign long-duration technologies establish bankable leadership or domestic demonstrations fail.

actors.memory: It knows China has ample manufacturing capacity and a large installed base, and believes the next test is whether provincial markets can dispatch storage productively and compensate duration.

actors.name: National Energy Administration of China
actors.role: China's energy regulator, official storage-statistics authority, and enforcer of grid-connection, dispatch, telemetry, utilization, and safety requirements.
actors.stance: Requires storage stations to become observable, measurable, controllable, responsive to dispatch, and compliant with lifecycle safety and market-registration rules.

salience.basis: It controls the official operational definition, compliance regime, and market-registration conditions for China's storage fleet.

actors.description: The National Energy Administration is China's national energy regulator and publisher of the official 136 GW/351 GWh end-2025 new-type-storage series.
goals: Ensure storage capacity is genuinely commissioned and dispatchable.
Increase utilization while maintaining safety and grid-code compliance.
Standardize operational data and enforce dispatch accountability.
constraints: Provincial reporting and project definitions are not fully harmonized.
Public data lack granular provincial revenue and charge-discharge information.
Rapid deployment increases inspection and enforcement burdens.
assets: Ability to remove non-compliant assets from market participation
vulnerabilities: The 136 GW official total conflicts with CNESA's 144.7 GW figure.
Headline utilization hours do not prove project-level profitability.
Safety incidents or telemetry failures could force a deployment slowdown.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: The NEA continues to report rapid scale growth, but its newer rules reveal a shift toward stricter operational discipline and away from treating installed megawatts as sufficient evidence of success.

beliefs: Storage has system value only when the grid can monitor and control it.
The next phase requires higher-quality operation rather than unqualified capacity growth.
worldview.identity: Operational regulator and custodian of China's storage statistics.
worldview.frame: Commissioning, telemetry, and utilization are the bridge from industrial policy to grid value.

incentives.driver: Credible implementation of national storage policy
incentives.gains_if: Official capacity targets are met with rising utilization and few major incidents.
incentives.loses_if: Reported capacity proves unavailable, unsafe, or economically idle.

resources: Coordination with grid companies and provincial administrations
actors.memory: It has observed rapid capacity growth, a rise in four-hour-plus projects, and improving utilization, but also knows that statistical boundaries and provincial implementation remain inconsistent.

actors.name: State Grid Corporation of China
actors.role: The dominant Chinese grid operator whose connection approvals, dispatch commands, telemetry acceptance, and utilization practices determine whether installed storage becomes an operating system resource.
actors.stance: Supports controllable, grid-connected storage that follows dispatch instructions and contributes to renewable integration, reliability, and ancillary services.

salience.basis: It operates most of China's transmission system and can translate national policy into actual connection, dispatch, and utilization.

actors.description: State Grid Corporation of China is the state-owned transmission and distribution utility serving most of mainland China.
goals: Integrate growing renewable generation without compromising reliability.
Use storage as a dispatchable flexibility and grid-forming resource.
Standardize telemetry and operating performance across provincial systems.
constraints: Provincial market rules and compensation mechanisms differ.
Congestion and renewable profiles vary across the network.
Large volumes of short-duration storage may offer diminishing incremental value.
vulnerabilities: Underutilized storage would expose inefficient capital allocation.
Telemetry or fire incidents could create reliability and political costs.
Inadequate duration could leave longer net-load gaps unresolved.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: State Grid's operating data show higher utilization, but the continued need for stronger telemetry and market-registration rules indicates that a material portion of the fleet has not yet reached uniform dispatch quality.

beliefs: Storage value depends on dispatch performance rather than installed nameplate alone.
Grid-forming capability and telemetry are increasingly necessary as renewable penetration rises.
worldview.identity: System operator responsible for converting storage investment into reliable grid flexibility.
worldview.frame: Storage is useful when it behaves as controllable network infrastructure.

incentives.gains_if: Storage reduces curtailment and peak stress while obeying dispatch.
incentives.loses_if: Storage is unavailable during stress periods or adds operational complexity without measurable benefits.

actors.memory: It knows equivalent utilization increased to 1,175 hours on its grid in 2025, but also knows that duration, location, and provincial revenue rules determine whether that improvement is durable.

actors.name: Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited
actors.role: A globally leading battery manufacturer whose LFP scale and 40 GWh sodium-ion expansion can materially influence chemistry costs, availability, and the timing of sodium-ion commercialization.
actors.stance: Continues to scale lithium-based batteries while investing heavily in sodium-ion as a complementary platform rather than publicly abandoning LFP.

salience.basis: Its manufacturing scale and disclosed 40 GWh sodium-ion line give it direct leverage over both the incumbent chemistry and its most credible near-term substitute.

actors.description: CATL is a major Chinese battery-cell manufacturer serving electric-vehicle and stationary-storage markets.
goals: Defend global cell leadership and LFP economics.
Establish sodium-ion as a commercial hedge and addressable niche platform.
Maintain access to export markets despite tariffs and local-content rules.
constraints: Announced nameplate capacity does not guarantee accepted commercial shipments.
Utility-scale sodium-ion lacks a 100 MWh-class independent operating reference.
FEOC, tariff, carbon-footprint, and local-content rules constrain market access.
vulnerabilities: Dependence on Chinese processing and manufacturing creates trade-policy exposure.
Industry overcapacity can pressure margins and warranty reserves.
Failure to convert sodium-ion capacity into operating projects would weaken its diversification narrative.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: CATL's sodium-ion investment signals a serious hedge, but its revealed commercial base remains overwhelmingly lithium-based and the disclosed 40 GWh line is capacity, not commissioned grid deployment.

beliefs: LFP remains the default stationary chemistry, but sodium-ion can win where safety, cold performance, or supply-chain policy matters.
Commercial advantage comes from scaling complete manufacturing ecosystems rather than laboratory chemistry alone.
worldview.identity: Incumbent battery leader hedging across chemistries.
worldview.frame: New chemistry should complement and extend the existing manufacturing franchise, not prematurely replace it.

incentives.gains_if: LFP deployment grows rapidly and sodium-ion opens additional niches.
incentives.loses_if: Trade barriers exclude Chinese content or non-lithium competitors establish bankable long-duration leadership.

incentives.gains_if: The Fujian line ships accepted cells into commercial projects from 2027 onward.
incentives.loses_if: The line remains underutilized or sodium systems fail warranty and efficiency tests.

actors.memory: CATL knows LFP benefits from a mature bankability stack and treats sodium-ion as an option whose credibility will be determined by shipment, warranty, and operating data rather than announced gigawatt-hours.

actors.name: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
actors.role: The US federal regulator whose interconnection, wholesale-market, and tariff decisions govern most ISO/RTO storage development outside ERCOT.
actors.stance: Supports cluster-based interconnection studies, stronger project-readiness requirements, withdrawal penalties, and broader participation of storage and distributed resources in wholesale markets.

salience.basis: Its orders determine queue rules and market access for most US regions, directly affecting whether announced projects can reach operation.

actors.description: FERC is the independent US federal agency regulating interstate transmission and wholesale electricity markets.
goals: Reduce speculative interconnection requests and accelerate viable projects.
Maintain non-discriminatory wholesale-market access.
Improve market participation for storage and distributed resources.
constraints: ERCOT is largely outside FERC wholesale-market jurisdiction.
Implementation depends on ISO/RTO tariff filings and utility compliance.
Cluster reform cannot eliminate transmission scarcity or network-upgrade costs.
assets: Jurisdiction over interstate transmission and organized wholesale markets
vulnerabilities: Developers may continue over-submitting into clusters.
Reform may raise attrition without shortening total time to operation.
Litigation and implementation delays can weaken rule effectiveness.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: FERC presents cluster reform as a route to faster, more orderly interconnection, but the dossier indicates that surviving projects still face network costs, site-control requirements, and multi-year implementation delays.

beliefs: Stronger readiness requirements and cluster studies can improve the quality of interconnection pipelines.
Market access should be technology-neutral within reliability constraints.
worldview.identity: Federal arbiter of transmission and wholesale-market rules.
worldview.frame: Storage deployment is primarily a market-access and transmission-planning problem once technology is commercially available.

incentives.gains_if: Viable projects progress faster and speculative queue volume declines.
incentives.loses_if: Lead times remain near five years and completion rates remain around historical lows.

actors.memory: FERC knows the US queue greatly exceeds plausible construction and that rule changes must distinguish mature projects from speculative applications without blocking needed capacity.

actors.name: European Commission
actors.role: The EU executive that sets battery sustainability rules, industrial-policy targets, permitting frameworks, and the regulatory perimeter affecting storage deployment and imported systems.
actors.stance: Supports accelerated storage deployment, approximately 40% EU manufacturing capacity for strategic net-zero technologies by 2030, and phased carbon-footprint, due-diligence, performance, and recycling requirements.

salience.basis: It can alter project costs, supply-chain eligibility, and permitting across the EU while the region faces a large gap between operating capacity and modeled 2030 need.

actors.description: The European Commission is the executive institution of the European Union and the originator of EU battery and net-zero industrial regulation.
goals: Expand storage to support electrification and renewable integration.
Build an EU manufacturing base and reduce strategic dependencies.
Enforce lifecycle sustainability, traceability, and recycling.
constraints: Distribution-grid connection rules remain fragmented across member states.
Dual network charges and long DSO queues can negate faster equipment permitting.
Local-content and sustainability rules can raise costs before domestic capacity scales.
vulnerabilities: A modeled 200 GW need is not a binding deployment mandate.
Only about 55 GW was operating or scheduled by end-2026 in the dossier's cited estimate.
Higher compliance costs could slow projects while failing to displace Chinese upstream dependence.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: The Commission seeks both rapid deployment and domestic industrial resilience, but the revealed near-term trade-off is that stricter sourcing and sustainability rules may raise delivered costs before European supply and grid access expand.

beliefs: Storage is essential to electrification but should not deepen uncontrolled supply-chain dependence.
Common product rules can shape global manufacturing practices.
worldview.identity: Regional regulator combining climate policy with industrial strategy.
worldview.frame: Deployment quality, domestic capability, and environmental compliance matter alongside gigawatts.

incentives.gains_if: Storage expands quickly while a credible European supply chain emerges.
incentives.loses_if: Connection queues persist and compliance costs leave the EU dependent on imports without achieving deployment targets.

actors.memory: The Commission knows equipment availability alone will not close the deployment gap and views network access, bankable revenue, and strategic supply chains as simultaneous policy problems.

actors.name: U.S. Department of Energy
actors.role: The US federal institution setting long-duration-storage cost and performance targets and supporting demonstrations, manufacturing, and commercialization.
actors.stance: Promotes commercial lift-off for intra-day and multi-day storage, with 2030 targets of US$650/kW and 75% round-trip efficiency for intra-day systems and US$1,100/kW with 55–60% efficiency for multi-day systems.

salience.basis: Its funding, targets, and manufacturing programs can determine whether non-lithium technologies cross from demonstration into bankable commercial reference projects.

actors.description: The U.S. Department of Energy is the federal department funding and coordinating energy research, demonstrations, manufacturing, and commercialization policy.
goals: Create commercially credible intra-day and multi-day storage technologies.
Reach approximately 3 GW/year of selected LDES manufacturing by 2030 and 10–15 GW/year by 2035.
Generate operating data that supports project finance and domestic supply chains.
constraints: Cost and efficiency goals are targets rather than delivered commercial results.
Projects still require long-duration revenue contracts, tax credits, or 24/7 clean-energy demand.
Federal demonstrations cannot by themselves create ISO capacity accreditation.
vulnerabilities: Delayed projects or weak operating data would make the 2030 targets appear aspirational.
Changes in tax policy and appropriations can interrupt commercialization.
Low-cycle assets may remain uneconomic despite low energy-media costs.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: DOE presents a pathway to LDES lift-off, while its own benchmarks reveal large remaining cost and efficiency gaps and dependence on contracted revenue.

beliefs: Demonstration data and manufacturing scale can reduce bankability barriers.
Long-duration storage needs policy support because merchant markets underprice infrequent reliability value.
worldview.identity: Technology-development principal attempting to bridge laboratory performance and commercial finance.
worldview.frame: LDES is a commercialization and market-formation challenge, not only a research problem.

incentives.driver: Commercial success of federally supported LDES
incentives.gains_if: Several non-lithium routes commission large projects with independently verified performance.
incentives.loses_if: The demonstration cohort slips and no route reaches repeatable project finance.

actors.memory: DOE knows current best-in-class LDES remains well above its 2030 targets and believes demonstrations must establish performance, warranty, and revenue evidence together.

actors.name: BYD Company Limited
actors.role: A vertically integrated Chinese cell and BESS supplier whose export scale, integration capability, and Saudi project frameworks reinforce the global LFP system moat.
actors.stance: Promotes turnkey, large-scale battery systems and long-term service packages for rapid grid deployment in China and export markets.

salience.basis: It is a leading Chinese BESS integrator with the ability to bundle cells, systems, controls, EPC support, and export-scale delivery.

actors.description: BYD is a Chinese battery, electric-vehicle, and energy-storage manufacturer and system integrator.
goals: Increase global BESS shipment and integration share.
Convert large frameworks, including Saudi projects, into commissioned capacity.
Defend turnkey cost leadership despite trade barriers.
constraints: Framework agreements are not equivalent to commercial operation.
US and EU sourcing rules can restrict Chinese-origin content.
Hot-climate projects require reliable thermal management and long-term warranties.
vulnerabilities: Tariffs and FEOC restrictions
Margin pressure from Chinese overcapacity
Execution risk on very large overseas frameworks
Dependence on LFP-dominant demand
actors.stated_vs_revealed: BYD's large international frameworks demonstrate commercial reach, but disclosed gigawatt-hours must still be discounted until projects reach commercial operation.

beliefs: Turnkey integration and service history are stronger competitive advantages than cell chemistry alone.
Long-term sovereign or utility contracts can offset technology and financing risk.
worldview.identity: Integrated battery manufacturer and global project supplier.
worldview.frame: The winning storage platform is the complete financed and warrantied system.

incentives.gains_if: Four-hour contracted procurement expands across China, the Gulf, Latin America, and other export markets.
incentives.loses_if: Local-content rules fragment manufacturing or large framework projects slip.

actors.memory: BYD knows Chinese integration scale is a bankability moat and that its overseas position depends on converting framework volume into commissioned, reliable assets.

actors.name: PJM Interconnection
actors.role: A major US regional transmission organization whose capacity auctions and accreditation rules can make four-hour or longer-duration storage financeable.
actors.stance: Uses capacity-market procurement and performance accreditation to secure resource adequacy, with recent auction outcomes making capacity revenue a central storage value stream.

salience.basis: Its auction prices and qualification rules directly determine whether storage in the Eastern Interconnection can support debt service.

actors.description: PJM Interconnection is the regional transmission organization and capacity-market operator serving much of the eastern United States.
goals: Procure sufficient reliable capacity.
Accredit storage according to availability and system need.
Move viable projects through reformed interconnection processes.
constraints: Its tariffs remain subject to FERC approval.
High capacity prices face political and consumer scrutiny.
A large storage queue can eventually cannibalize capacity value.
vulnerabilities: A future capacity-price collapse could undermine new storage finance.
Queue congestion may prevent qualified projects from reaching operation.
Rules that cap useful duration too low would deter 10-hour-plus systems.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: PJM's reliability framework is technology-neutral in principle, but the revealed economics depend heavily on how four-hour-class resources are accredited and whether auction scarcity persists.

beliefs: Capacity should be paid according to dependable contribution during system stress.
Energy and ancillary revenue alone may not support sufficient firm capacity.
worldview.identity: Capacity-market arbiter and regional reliability coordinator.
worldview.frame: Storage value is its dependable contribution at scarcity hours, not just its energy arbitrage.

incentives.gains_if: Auctions attract dependable resources without sustained excessive prices.
incentives.loses_if: Prices collapse before enough new capacity arrives or remain politically unsustainable.

actors.memory: PJM knows recent scarcity pricing can underwrite storage, but also knows that growing qualified supply may reproduce the revenue cannibalization observed in ERCOT.

actors.name: Electric Reliability Council of Texas
actors.role: The Texas system operator and energy-market administrator whose RTC+B implementation and scarcity-price design provide the leading test of merchant battery economics without a conventional capacity market.
actors.stance: Continues to integrate batteries through energy, ancillary-service, and real-time co-optimization reforms rather than adopting a PJM-style capacity market.

salience.basis: ERCOT is the clearest live market test of whether storage can remain financeable after ancillary services saturate.

actors.description: ERCOT is the independent system operator and wholesale-market administrator for most of Texas.
goals: Maintain reliability in a rapidly changing generation mix.
Improve real-time co-optimization of batteries through RTC+B.
Preserve efficient scarcity and ancillary-service price signals.
constraints: ERCOT lacks a conventional forward capacity market.
Battery entry has already compressed ancillary and arbitrage revenue.
It is largely outside FERC wholesale-market jurisdiction.
vulnerabilities: Average battery revenue fell from about US$192/kW-year in 2023 to about US$55/kW-year in 2024.
Continued revenue weakness could halt merchant projects despite strong technical need.
A reliability event could trigger politically driven market redesign.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: ERCOT relies on energy and ancillary markets to reveal value, but the observed revenue collapse shows that the existing design underpays incremental identical batteries once services saturate.

beliefs: Co-optimized real-time prices should guide flexible-resource behavior.
Administrative long-term capacity contracts are not the default solution.
worldview.identity: Energy-only market operator testing whether merchant incentives can support storage at scale.
worldview.frame: Storage should earn from real-time system value, even though fleet growth can erode that value.

incentives.driver: Reliable operation without a conventional capacity market
incentives.gains_if: RTC+B improves dispatch and restores adequate investment signals.
incentives.loses_if: Revenue remains too low for new projects or a reliability event forces major redesign.

actors.memory: ERCOT knows batteries can saturate shallow service markets rapidly and treats post-RTC+B revenue as the decisive evidence on whether its market design remains investable.

actors.name: National Energy System Operator
actors.role: Great Britain's system planner and operator associated in the dossier with a cap-and-floor framework intended to make eight-hour-plus storage bankable.
actors.stance: Supports regulated revenue floors and caps for qualifying long-duration projects where merchant operating history is insufficient for project finance.

salience.basis: Its long-duration procurement and planning framework can create the long-tenor cash flows needed for the UK's first commercial reference projects.

actors.description: The National Energy System Operator is Great Britain's independent electricity and gas system planning and operating organization.
goals: Procure flexibility and reliability for a renewables-heavy power system.
Enable bankable long-duration projects through regulated revenue support.
Develop operating evidence for technologies beyond lithium-ion.
constraints: Final eligibility, cap, floor, and award parameters determine bankability.
Regulated support can attract expensive projects if competition is weak.
Technology performance remains uncertain before long operating records exist.
vulnerabilities: Undersubscribed or expensive procurement would weaken the UK reference model.
Project delays would postpone evidence for liquid-air and other LDES routes.
Poor performance could transfer risk to consumers.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: The cap-and-floor approach recognizes that merchant markets do not yet finance long-duration storage, effectively substituting regulated revenue for missing operating and warranty history.

beliefs: Long-duration reliability value requires a contractual floor.
Reference projects are necessary before merchant finance can emerge.
worldview.identity: System planner and market intermediary creating a bankability bridge for LDES.
worldview.frame: Revenue certainty is the missing infrastructure for long-duration deployment.

incentives.gains_if: Projects commission at competitive cost and meet availability requirements.
incentives.loses_if: Contracts socialize costs without producing dependable capacity.

actors.name: Terna S.p.A.
actors.role: Italy's transmission system operator and administrator of the MACSE framework, a major European test of contracted revenue for multi-hour storage.
actors.stance: Supports technology-neutral, long-tenor procurement of storage capacity to meet system adequacy and renewable-integration needs.

actors.description: Terna is Italy's national electricity transmission system operator.
goals: Procure storage capacity suited to Italy's renewable and adequacy needs.
Create competitive long-term cash flows for multi-hour resources.
Avoid overdependence on short-duration merchant batteries.

worldview.identity: National utility responsible for turning procurement scale into operating reliability.
worldview.frame: Commissioned and dispatchable gigawatt-hours matter more than framework size.

incentives.gains_if: The BYD projects reach COD and deliver contracted availability.
incentives.loses_if: Schedule, thermal, or integration failures leave announced capacity unavailable.

actors.memory: SEC knows the portfolio is globally significant on paper and that its value depends on synchronized construction, grid integration, and long-term service performance.

actors.name: Solar Energy Corporation of India
actors.role: India's federal renewable-energy procurement intermediary, responsible for long-term storage tenders and structures intended to bridge the country's tender-to-commissioning gap.
actors.stance: Supports larger four-hour storage products, 15-year contracts, and viability-gap funding to accelerate commissioned BESS capacity.

salience.basis: Its tender and contract design can determine whether India's roughly 102 GWh of tendered storage converts into operating capacity.

actors.description: Solar Energy Corporation of India is a state-owned federal implementing and procurement agency for renewable energy and storage.
aliases: Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited
goals: Convert awarded storage projects into commissioned capacity.
Move procurement toward four-hour products suited to evening peaks.
Use long-term contracts and viability-gap funding to lower tariffs.
constraints: State DISCOM credit quality and payment risk.
Connection-charge and open-access uncertainty.
Aggressive bids may depend on future cost declines or refinancing.
vulnerabilities: Approximately 102 GWh tendered versus about 0.5 GWh commissioned exposes an execution gap.
Low bids may not remain financeable.
DISCOM and interconnection delays can strand awarded projects.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: SECI's tender volumes signal aggressive ambition, but revealed commissioning remains far below awards, indicating that offtake credit and execution are more binding than equipment availability.

beliefs: Centralized procurement and viability support can overcome early storage costs.
Four-hour contracts better match India's emerging system need than earlier two-hour products.
worldview.identity: Federal market maker attempting to turn tender scale into operational storage.
worldview.frame: The central challenge is contract and commissioning discipline, not a shortage of bids.

incentives.gains_if: Awarded projects close financing, connect, and deliver at contracted tariffs.
incentives.loses_if: The pipeline remains large while commissioned capacity stays negligible.

actors.memory: SECI knows India has enough tendered volume to meet a meaningful share of future needs but that DISCOM credit, connection rules, and aggressive bidding can prevent COD.

actors.name: Australian Energy Market Operator
actors.role: Australia's electricity-market and system planner, whose Integrated System Plan determines the expected mix of batteries, pumped hydro, transmission, and deeper storage.
actors.stance: Plans for approximately 40 GW of utility-scale storage by 2050, with the largest share in four-to-twelve-hour batteries and a smaller pumped-hydro contribution.

salience.basis: Its system plan and reliability requirements shape procurement after major Australian pumped-hydro projects were shelved, cancelled, or re-costed.

actors.description: The Australian Energy Market Operator operates the National Electricity Market and publishes the Integrated System Plan.
goals: Maintain reliability through coal retirement and renewable expansion.
Identify an efficient mix of batteries, transmission, pumped hydro, and deeper storage.
Avoid overreliance on delayed megaprojects.
constraints: AEMO plans do not themselves guarantee project finance or construction.
Transmission delivery and social license remain binding.
Pumped-hydro cost overruns narrow the available deep-storage options.
vulnerabilities: Battery-heavy substitution for pumped hydro may leave multi-day reliability gaps.
Transmission delays could invalidate the optimal development path.
Planning assumptions may lag rapid behind-the-meter battery adoption.
actors.stated_vs_revealed: AEMO retains pumped hydro in the long-term mix, but recent project cancellations and cost escalation reveal a practical shift toward modular batteries and selective non-PHES long-duration options.

beliefs: Storage duration must match the evolving reliability gap.
Modular batteries can substitute for some civil megaprojects but not necessarily all deep-storage needs.
worldview.identity: System planner balancing executable projects against long-term reliability requirements.
worldview.frame: The optimal technology is the one that can be delivered with its required transmission and reliability contribution.

incentives.gains_if: Storage and transmission commission in time to replace retiring generation.
incentives.loses_if: Pumped-hydro failures or battery duration shortfalls produce reliability gaps.

actors.memory: AEMO knows batteries are deploying faster than earlier assumptions while pumped-hydro execution has weakened, forcing closer scrutiny of four-to-twelve-hour and multi-day adequacy.

actors.name: Form Energy
actors.role: The leading iron-air developer in the dossier, attempting to commercialize approximately 100-hour storage and provide a non-lithium option for cross-day and multi-day reliability.
actors.stance: Argues that low-cost iron-air energy modules can economically serve 100-hour reliability needs that daily-cycling lithium batteries cannot.

salience.basis: Its projects are the dossier's leading indicator for whether metal-air storage can cross from pre-commercial demonstrations into repeatable utility deployment.

actors.description: Form Energy is a US energy-storage company developing rechargeable iron-air batteries designed for multi-day discharge.
goals: Commission utility projects with Georgia Power, Xcel Energy, and Great River Energy on schedule.
Demonstrate dependable 100-hour operation and bankable warranties.
Scale manufacturing sufficiently to reduce system cost.
constraints: The technology remains pre-commercial at grid scale as of the cutoff.
Round-trip efficiency is far below LFP.
Low cycle frequency requires long-term capacity revenue rather than energy arbitrage.
vulnerabilities: Commissioning delays
Failure to achieve availability or efficiency claims
Insufficient 15-year revenue contracts
High power-side capex relative to low annual throughput
actors.stated_vs_revealed: Form presents iron-air as a commercial multi-day solution, but the revealed evidence base remains limited commercial deployment without the multi-year operating record required for broad non-recourse finance.

beliefs: Lithium-ion is structurally expensive for 100-hour storage.
Low efficiency can be acceptable when renewable charging energy is abundant and reliability value is contracted.
worldview.identity: Technology challenger seeking to create the iron-air asset class.
worldview.frame: The relevant competition is firm multi-day capacity, not daily four-hour arbitrage.

incentives.gains_if: Projects commission and publish credible availability data under long-term utility contracts.
incentives.loses_if: Projects slip or fail to meet efficiency and availability expectations.

actors.memory: Form knows it does not need to beat LFP at four hours, but must prove that low-cost energy capacity and contracted reliability outweigh low efficiency and limited operating history.

actors.name: Hydrostor
actors.role: A leading advanced compressed-air developer attempting to establish a bankable 8–24-hour reference class through large projects such as the 300 MW/2,100 MWh Apex project.
actors.stance: Promotes advanced compressed-air storage as a fuel-free, long-life alternative for long-duration applications where suitable sites and long-term contracts exist.

salience.basis: A successful large Hydrostor project would materially improve the bankability of compressed-air storage, while failure would reinforce its niche status.

actors.description: Hydrostor is a Canadian long-duration-storage developer specializing in advanced compressed-air energy storage.
goals: Deliver a utility-scale A-CAES reference project.
Secure long-tenor tolling or capacity contracts.
Demonstrate approximately 60–65% round-trip efficiency and reliable thermal management.
constraints: Site geology and cavern availability
Long permitting and construction schedules
Unproven large-scale thermal-store cycle record
Need for Tier-1 EPC and long-term contracted revenue
vulnerabilities: Civil-works overruns
Project delay
Failure to validate thermal management over repeated cycles
Dependence on location-specific infrastructure
actors.stated_vs_revealed: Hydrostor argues that A-CAES is commercially ready, but the dossier finds no independently measured unit with the required large-scale, thousand-cycle operating history.

beliefs: Compressed-air storage can outperform electrochemical systems at longer durations.
Geology and contracts, rather than the thermodynamic cycle alone, determine commercial success.
worldview.identity: Infrastructure-scale challenger seeking to revive compressed-air storage with modern thermal management.
worldview.frame: The asset should be compared with long-lived grid infrastructure, not short-lived battery containers.

incentives.gains_if: Apex or an equivalent project reaches COD within budget and achieves warranted performance.
incentives.loses_if: Civil, permitting, or performance problems repeat the execution record of other megaprojects.

actors.memory: Hydrostor knows the architecture has duration advantages but that financiers will judge it primarily on construction execution, independent operating data, and contract tenor.

actors.name: Highview Power
actors.role: The leading liquid-air storage developer in the dossier, using UK regulated revenue support to move from a 50 MW demonstrator toward a proposed 300 MW commercial project.
actors.stance: Promotes liquid-air storage as a modular, non-lithium technology based on established turbomachinery and suitable for multi-hour grid service.

salience.basis: Its UK projects are a direct test of whether a cap-and-floor mechanism can overcome limited cycle and warranty history for liquid-air storage.

actors.description: Highview Power is a UK energy-storage developer commercializing liquid-air energy storage.
goals: Finance and commission a large UK liquid-air project.
Demonstrate repeatable availability and efficiency under a regulated revenue framework.
Establish a bankable supply chain based on conventional turbomachinery.
constraints: Round-trip efficiency is approximately 50–60%.
No commercial unit has a decade-scale operating and warranty record.
Cryogenic equipment and project capex require long-term revenue support.
vulnerabilities: Dependence on cap-and-floor terms
Project delays or cost escalation
Failure to establish long-term cycle performance
Competition from batteries and compressed-air systems
actors.stated_vs_revealed: Highview emphasizes modularity and established components, but the use of regulated revenue support reveals that conventional project finance does not yet accept the technology's operating-history risk.

beliefs: Established industrial equipment can shorten the path to bankability.
Regulated revenue support can compensate temporarily for a thin operating record.
worldview.identity: Liquid-air technology challenger seeking a first repeatable commercial reference.
worldview.frame: The commercial bottleneck is warranty and financeability rather than basic thermodynamics.

incentives.gains_if: The large project reaches COD and performs within the cap-and-floor regime.
incentives.loses_if: The project slips, exceeds capex expectations, or fails cycle-performance tests.

actors.memory: Highview knows debt providers view regulated revenue as a substitute for missing operating history and must convert that support into independently verified performance.

key_events.event: Lithium-ion battery packs were priced at roughly US$1,400/kWh, establishing the starting point for the subsequent approximately 90% cost decline.
Sumitomo Electric and Hokkaido Electric commissioned the 60 MW/252 MWh Yusaku vanadium-redox system, which became the principal decade-class flow-battery reference.
The Hokkaido flow-battery reference was expanded to approximately 60 MW/510 MWh.
FERC issued Order 2023, shifting US interconnection procedures toward cluster studies, stronger readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties.
Average ERCOT battery revenue fell to about US$55/kW-year from approximately US$192/kW-year in 2023, demonstrating rapid ancillary-service and arbitrage cannibalization.
The Moss Landing battery fire intensified scrutiny of siting, emergency response, insurance, and NFPA 855 compliance.
China published its 2025–2027 new-type-storage scale-up action plan, targeting at least 180 GW by 2027 and approximately RMB 250 billion of direct investment.
China published Document 1360, framing storage as a controllable system resource subject to dispatch and telemetry requirements.
ERCOT implemented RTC+B, creating a live test of whether real-time co-optimization can restore storage revenue without a conventional capacity market.
Global battery additions reached 112 GW/307 GWh, while China ended the year with an official 136 GW/351 GWh of new-type storage.
The National Energy Administration reported China's 136 GW/351 GWh stock, 96.1% lithium-ion share, 2.58-hour average duration, 27.6% four-hour-plus share, and 1,195 equivalent utilization hours.
BloombergNEF projected 158 GW of global battery additions in 2026, rising to 308 GW in 2036, and framed a 3.8 TW cumulative station-scale-storage trajectory by 2035.

contested_claims.claim: China had either 136 GW or 144.7 GW of cumulative new-type storage at end-2025.

positions.stance: The National Energy Administration reported 136 GW and 351 GWh of built-and-operational new-type storage.
sources: NEA press conference on 2025 new-type storage

positions.stance: CNESA reported 144.7 GW cumulative, equal to 51.9% of the global total.
sources: China Releases Official Energy Storage Report Highlighting 130% Growth in Installed Capacity
Year-End Review 2025: China's New-Type Energy Storage Installed Capacity Surpasses 100 GW

contested_claims.why_they_differ: The likely causes are cutoff timing and different treatment of commissioned, grid-connected, and demonstration projects; the dossier uses 136 GW as the resolution anchor and does not average the figures.

contested_claims.claim: The relevant 2025–2026 four-hour battery cost benchmark is either about US$78/MWh or US$210–292/MWh.

positions.stance: BloombergNEF reported an approximately US$78/MWh global four-hour battery LCOE, down 27% year-on-year.
sources: Energy Storage Enters the 100-Gigawatt Era: Three Things to Know

positions.stance: Lazard reported a US-focused unsubsidized four-hour LCOS range of US$210–292/MWh.
sources: Lazard Releases 2025 Levelized Cost of Energy+ Report

contested_claims.why_they_differ: The figures use different geographies, financing assumptions, tariff cases, charging-cost treatment, and LCOE-versus-LCOS definitions; they are not like-for-like cost observations.

contested_claims.claim: Sodium-ion has already reached commercially significant grid-scale deployment.

positions.stance: CATL disclosed a 40 GWh Fujian sodium-ion expansion and HiNa describes sodium-ion as entering the commercial era.
sources: CATL to add 40 GWh of sodium-ion battery capacity in $735m Fujian expansion
Sodium-Ion Batteries Enter the Commercial Era

positions.stance: The available shipment data remain overwhelmingly LFP-dominated and do not identify a 100 MWh-class sodium reference project with independent operating data.
sources: 2025 BESS cell and system shipments: BYD takes BESS crown, no Korean firms in top 10 cell suppliers
Lithium-Ion Batteries are set to Face Competition from Novel Tech for Long-Duration Storage

contested_claims.why_they_differ: Vendors report nameplate capacity, production plans, and framework agreements, whereas the skeptical position requires commissioned projects, accepted cells, independent performance data, and bankable warranties.

contested_claims.claim: Global storage is on a trajectory consistent with approximately 1,500 GW by 2030.

positions.stance: The IEA Net Zero Emissions pathway requires about 1,500 GW of total grid-scale storage by 2030, including roughly 1,200 GW of batteries.
sources: Executive summary – Batteries and Secure Energy Transitions

positions.stance: BloombergNEF's expected-build trajectory reaches approximately 3.8 TW of cumulative station-scale storage only by 2035.
sources: Energy Storage Enters the 100-Gigawatt Era: Three Things to Know

contested_claims.why_they_differ: The IEA number is a normative net-zero requirement with a broader boundary, while BloombergNEF is an expected deployment outlook under stated policy; the figures should not be treated as competing forecasts with identical scope.

contested_claims.claim: The dossier's four global scenario probabilities are stable and unambiguous.

positions.stance: Section 16 assigns 30% to Lithium Dominance, 25% to LDES Diversified, 20% to China-Centric Vertical, and 25% to Stagnation.
The chart-ready V7 table assigns 47% to high-growth lithium dominance, 29% to high-growth diversification, 18% to low-growth lithium dominance, and 6% to low-growth LDES leap.

contested_claims.why_they_differ: The probability weights drifted between the narrative scenario block and the later 2×2 chart restatement even though both purport to describe the same annual-additions and non-lithium-share axes; this extraction preserves Section 16 as primary and flags the inconsistency.
